title: Morphology-Aware Rule Catalog: Bengali L1 Transfer in Hindi L2
corpus: IIT Kharagpur campus staff, 8 speakers (4F/4M), 42.8 min, 3965 words

rules.name: Masculine Default on Feminine Nouns
rules.description: Speakers use masculine verb forms with feminine nouns, regardless of the noun's grammatical gender.
rules.l1_explanation: Bengali has no grammatical gender. Hindi requires verb agreement with noun gender. Speakers default to the unmarked (masculine) form.

rules.name: Masculine Default in Self-Reference (Female Speakers)
rules.description: Female speakers use masculine verb forms when talking about themselves.
rules.l1_explanation: Bengali verbs do not inflect for the gender of the subject. Hindi requires verb-subject gender agreement. Female Bengali L1 speakers carry over the gender-neutral pattern, defaulting to masculine.
rules.speaker_note: S2 (female) shows 0 self-referential errors — possible higher Hindi proficiency or awareness

rules.name: Ergative 'ne' Avoidance
rules.description: Complete avoidance of the Hindi ergative marker 'ne' in perfective constructions.
rules.l1_explanation: Bengali has no ergative case marking. In Hindi, the ergative 'ne' marks the agent of transitive perfective verbs, and the verb then agrees with the object rather than the subject. Bengali speakers avoid this entirely rather than producing incorrect forms.

examples.note: No 'ne' but verb still masculine (khana is M, so agreement happens to be correct)
S6 switches to Bengali entirely to avoid the construction
examples.speaker: S6

rules.note: This is an avoidance strategy, not an error. Speakers restructure sentences to bypass the construction entirely. Some switch to Bengali for these contexts.

rules.name: Bengali Lexical Insertion (Tag-switching)
rules.description: Single Bengali content words inserted into otherwise Hindi utterances, typically for household objects and everyday items.
rules.l1_explanation: These are high-frequency household terms where the Bengali word is more accessible than the Hindi equivalent. Follows Poplack (1980) tag-switching pattern.

rules.name: Bengali Inter-sentential Switching
rules.description: Full Bengali sentences or clauses inserted between Hindi utterances.
rules.l1_explanation: Speakers switch to Bengali for entire clauses, especially when describing familiar domestic scenes or when Hindi vocabulary is insufficient.

examples.meaning: I am Bengali, born in Kharagpur
examples.speaker: S6

rules.frequency: Most frequent in S6, who sits at the high-Bengali end of the proficiency gradient; S1 and S5 also produce inter-sentential switches

rules.name: Three-way Code-mixing
rules.description: Bengali, Hindi, and English elements combined within a single phrase.

examples.analysis: English instruction followed by Bengali noun
examples.speaker: S3

rules.note: Hindi-English mixing is common and unsurprising in this context. Bengali-English mixing within Hindi matrix is the distinctive pattern.

cross_cutting_patterns.proficiency_gradient: Error frequency correlates inversely with Hindi exposure. S4 (12 errors) learned Hindi later; S2 (0 errors) has longer Hindi exposure.
cross_cutting_patterns.unidirectionality: ALL gender errors are masculine-default. Zero instances of feminine-on-masculine. This is diagnostic of a language without grammatical gender (Bengali) influencing one that has it (Hindi).
cross_cutting_patterns.avoidance_over_error: For the ergative 'ne', speakers avoid the construction entirely (0/149) rather than producing incorrect forms. For gender, they produce errors rather than avoiding gendered constructions.
cross_cutting_patterns.whisper_interaction: Whisper silently corrects gender errors to standard Hindi and converts Bengali words to Hindi equivalents, making automated analysis unreliable for this research question.
